q-16227:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1)=\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

The sine function has a period of $2\pi .$ Hence, the general solution for the given equation is

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi .
$$

q-120762:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})={45}^{∘}
$$

Our first solution lies in the $1$st quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={45}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has ${\theta }_{R}={45}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13979076/assets/c722d4fa2b77011e4df5b086c19bb09943446941484cfaf87559ca39a52183bc.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$  lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={360}^{∘}-{45}^{∘} \\  & ={315}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution for the given equation is

$$
x={45}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘},\,x={315}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}.
$$

q-120771:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{arcsin}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4}
$$

Our first solution lies in the $1$st quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13979076/assets/269d503189ab1027c3d8028542ef0c6a0e2f146aef0f7916691428866ce1b894.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$  lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the given equation is

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi ,\,x=\frac{3\pi }{4}+2n\pi .
$$

q-76741:
Recall that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}+1} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\sqrt{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{arctan}(\sqrt{2}+1)=\frac{3\pi }{8}
$$

The tangent function has a period of $\pi .$  Hence, the general solution for the given equation is

$$
x=\frac{3\pi }{8}+n\pi .
$$

q-16245:

$$
{x}_{1}=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)=-\frac{\pi }{4}
$$

$$

q-65848:
The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{\pi }{6} & =\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & x+\frac{\pi }{6} & =\frac{2\pi }{3}+2\pi n.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi  & \, & \, & x & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{2\pi }{3}+2\pi n \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{6}+2n\pi  & \, & \, & x & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that $b=\frac{1}{2}.$

q-19756:
The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{3\pi }{4} & =0+2\pi n.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-\frac{3\pi }{4}+2\pi n \\ x & =-\frac{3\pi }{8}+\pi n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-\frac{3}{8}.$

q-42788:
First, note that the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4}+{20}^{∘})=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\frac{x}{4}+{20}^{∘}={60}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}\cdot n,\,\frac{x}{4}+{20}^{∘}={300}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}\cdot n.
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4}=-{20}^{∘}+{60}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}\cdot n, & \,\frac{x}{4}=-{20}^{∘}+{300}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}\cdot n \\ \frac{x}{4}={40}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}\cdot n, & \,\frac{x}{4}={280}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}\cdot n \\ x={160}^{∘}+1\,{440}^{∘}\cdot n, & \,x=1\,{120}^{∘}+1\,{440}^{∘}\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $a=160.$

q-42789:

q-78008:
First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{2{x}^{2}+x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(2+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(x+0)}{(2+0)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{x}{2} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

q-106705:
For large positive values of $x,$ we have $|{x}^{3}-5|=({x}^{3}-5).$ Consequently, for $x\to \infty ,$ we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{|{x}^{3}-5|}{2-{x}^{3}}={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{3}-5}{2-{x}^{3}}.
$$

The horizontal asymptote for $x>0$ is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{3}-5}{2-{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{5}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(1-\frac{5}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}-1)} \\  & =\frac{1-0}{0-1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-1.$

q-18280:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}A=|\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =5|\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|+3|\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5(0-2)+0+3(-2+3) \\  & =-10+0+3 \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{33}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{33}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{33} & =(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-15-0 \\  & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{33}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{33}=\frac{1}{-7}\cdot (-15)=\frac{15}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-8558:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{7\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-\frac{7\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{13\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{13\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(6n-13)\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=4$ gives $x=\frac{11\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=5$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=6$ gives $x=\frac{23\pi }{12}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{5\pi }{12},\,\frac{11\pi }{12},\,\frac{17\pi }{12},\,\frac{23\pi }{12}.
$$

Finally, since ${x}_{1}=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ and ${x}_{4}=\frac{23\pi }{12},$ we have

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{4}=\frac{5\pi }{12}+\frac{23\pi }{12}=\frac{28\pi }{12}=\frac{7\pi }{3}.
$$

q-8550:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\frac{\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(6n-1)\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x\le \pi .$

- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\frac{7\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{11\pi }{12}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x\le \pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=-\frac{7\pi }{12},\,-\frac{\pi }{12},\,\frac{5\pi }{12},\,\frac{11\pi }{12}.
$$

Finally, since ${x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{12}$ and ${x}_{3}=\frac{5\pi }{12},$ we have

$$
{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{5\pi }{12}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

q-121558:

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{\pi }{18}+\frac{n\pi }{3} \\ x & =\frac{(1+6n)\pi }{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{18}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{7\pi }{18}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{13\pi }{18}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ (written in ascending order) are 

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{18},\frac{7\pi }{18},\frac{13\pi }{18}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3} & =\frac{\pi }{18}+\frac{13\pi }{18} \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{18} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-51346:
**Step 1:** First, we write the inverse function implicitly. The given function is $y=5-10x,$ and to write the inverse function implicitly, we swap $x$ and $y$ as follows:

$$
x=5-10y
$$

Note that in the equation above, we have $y={h}^{-1}(x).$

**Step 2:** Next, we differentiate. The overall goal is to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ but the equation is already solved for $x,$ so we compute $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}$ and then take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(5-10y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =-10 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Lastly, we write the result in terms of ${h}^{-1}(x).$ Since $y={h}^{-1}(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{h}^{-1}(x)] & =-\frac{1}{10} \\ {({h}^{-1})}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$
